entries.0ea8f470ebca4f13284e87ab7293dc74c06bf95f: <div sID="gen652" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="Gen.18" sID="Gen.18"/> <div eID="gen652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen653" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen654" type="x-p"/> We have an account in this chapter of another interview between God and Abraham, probably within a few days after the former, as the reward of his cheerful obedience to the law of circumcision. Here is, I. The kind visit which God made him, and the kind entertainment which he gave to that visit, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.1-Gen.18.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. The matters discoursed of between them. 1. The purposes of God's love concerning Sarah, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.9-Gen.18.15">ver. 9-15</reference>. 2. The purposes of God's wrath concerning Sodom. (1.) The discovery God made to Abraham of his design to destroy Sodom, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.16-Gen.18.22">ver. 16-22</reference>. (2.) The intercession Abraham made for Sodom, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.23-Gen.18.33">ver. 23</reference>, &c.).
entries.dd1b5343eb6c7ae6a33bfa484b6497f78f36e5f2: <div eID="gen654" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen653" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Abraham's Interview with the Angels. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1898.)</title> <div sID="gen655" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> appeared unto him in the plains of Mamre: and he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day; <hi type="super">2</hi> And he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him: and when he saw <hi type="italic">them,</hi> he ran to meet them from the tent-door, and bowed himself toward the ground, <hi type="super">3</hi> And said, My Lord, if now I have found favour in thy sight, pass not away, I pray thee, from thy servant: <hi type="super">4</hi> Let a little water, I pray you, be fetched, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree: <hi type="super">5</hi> And I will fetch a morsel of bread, and comfort ye your hearts; after that ye shall pass on: for therefore are ye come to your servant. And they said, So do, as thou hast said. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Abraham hastened into the tent unto Sarah, and said, Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, knead <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and make cakes upon the hearth. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Abraham ran unto the herd, and fetched a calf tender and good, and gave <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto a young man; and he hasted to dress it. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he took butter, and milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set <hi type="italic">it</hi> before them; and he stood by them under the tree, and they did eat. <div eID="gen655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen656" type="x-p"/> The appearance of God to Abraham seems to have had in it more of freedom and familiarity, and less of grandeur and majesty, than those we have hitherto read of; and therefore more resembles that great visit which, in the fullness of time, the Son of God was to make to the world, when the Word would be flesh, and appear as one of us. Observe here, <div eID="gen656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen657" type="x-p"/> I. How Abraham expected strangers, and how richly his expectations were answered (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">He sat in the tent-door, in the heat of the day;</hi> not so much to repose or divert himself as to seek an opportunity of doing good, by giving entertainment to strangers and travellers, there being perhaps no inns to accommodate them. Note, 1. We are likely to have the most comfort of those good works to which we are most free and forward. 2. God graciously visits those in whom he has first raised the expectation of him, and manifests himself to those that wait for him. When Abraham was thus sitting, he saw three men coming towards him. These three men were three spiritual heavenly beings, now assuming human bodies, that they might be visible to Abraham, and conversable with him. Some think that they were all created angels, others that one of them was the Son of God, the angel of the covenant, whom Abraham distinguished from the rest (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.3">v. 3</reference>), and who is called <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.13">v. 13</reference>. The apostle improves this for the encouragement of hospitality, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.2">Heb. xiii. 2</reference>. Those that have been forward to entertain strangers have entertained angels, to their unspeakable honour and satisfaction. Where, upon a prudent and impartial judgment, we see no cause to suspect ill, charity teaches us to hope well and to show kindness accordingly. It is better to feed five drones, or wasps, than to starve one bee. <div eID="gen657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen658" type="x-p"/> II. How Abraham entertained those strangers, and how kindly his entertainment was accepted. The Holy Ghost takes particular notice of the very free and affectionate welcome Abraham gave to the strangers. 1. He was very complaisant and respectful to them. Forgetting his age and gravity, he <hi type="italic">ran to meet them</hi> in the most obliging manner, and with all due courtesy <hi type="italic">bowed himself towards the ground,</hi> though as yet he knew nothing of them but that they appeared graceful respectable men. Note, Religion does not destroy, but improve, good manners, and teaches us to honour all men. Decent civility is a great ornament to piety. 2. He was very earnest and importunate for their stay, and took it as a great favour, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.3-Gen.18.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. Note, (1.) It becomes those whom God has blessed with plenty to be liberal and open-hearted in their entertainments, according to their ability, and (not in compliment, but cordially) to bid their friends welcome. We should take a pleasure in showing kindness to any; for both God and man love a cheerful giver. Who would <hi type="italic">eat the bread of him that has an evil eye?</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.6-Prov.23.7">Prov. xxiii. 6, 7</reference>. (2.) Those that would have communion with God must earnestly desire it and pray for it. God is a guest worth entertaining. 3. His entertainment, though it was very free, was yet plain and homely, and there was nothing in it of the gaiety and niceness of our times. His dining-room was an arbour under a tree; no rich table-linen, no side-board set with plate. His feast was a joint or two of veal, and some cakes baked on the hearth, and both hastily dressed up. Here were no dainties, no varieties, no forced-meats, no sweet-meats, but good, plain, wholesome food, though Abraham was very rich and his guests were very honourable. Note, We ought not to be curious in our diet. Let us be thankful for food convenient, though it be homely and common; and not be desirous of dainties, for they are deceitful meat to those that love them and set their hearts upon them. 4. He and his wife were both of them very attentive and busy, in accommodating their guests with the best they had. Sarah herself is cook and baker; Abraham runs to fetch the calf, brings out the milk and butter, and thinks it not below him to wait at table, that he might show how heartily welcome his guests were. Note, (1.) Those that have real merit need not take state upon them, nor are their prudent condescensions any disparagement to them. (2.) Hearty friendship will stoop to any thing but sin. Christ himself has taught us to wash one another's feet, in humble love. Those that thus abase themselves shall be exalted. Here Abraham's faith showed itself in good works; and so must ours, else it is dead, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.21">Jam. ii. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.26">26</reference>. The father of the faithful was famous for charity, and generosity, and good house-keeping; and we must learn of him to <hi type="italic">do good and to communicate.</hi> Job did not eat his morsel alone, <reference osisRef="Job.31.17">Job xxxi. 17</reference>.
entries.4fd6b1a0be19a74190815668025cef1efad93bb3: <div eID="gen658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen659" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And they said unto him, Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> Sarah thy wife? And he said, Behold, in the tent. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he said, I will certainly return unto thee according to the time of life; and, lo, Sarah thy wife shall have a son. And Sarah heard <hi type="italic">it</hi> in the tent-door, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> behind him. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now Abraham and Sarah <hi type="italic">were</hi> old <hi type="italic">and</hi> well stricken in age; <hi type="italic">and</hi> it ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women. 12 Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also? <hi type="super">13</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Abraham, Wherefore did Sarah laugh, saying, Shall I of a surety bear a child, which am old? <hi type="super">14</hi> Is any thing too hard for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son. <hi type="super">15</hi> Then Sarah denied, saying, I laughed not; for she was afraid. And he said, Nay; but thou didst laugh. <div eID="gen659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen660" type="x-p"/> These heavenly guests (being sent to confirm the promise lately made to Abraham, that he should have a son by Sarah), while they are receiving Abraham's kind entertainment, they return his kindness. He receives angels, and has angels' rewards, a gracious message from heaven, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.41">Matt. x. 41</reference>. <div eID="gen660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen661" type="x-p"/> I. Care is taken that Sarah should be within hearing. She must conceive by faith, and therefore the promise must be made to her, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.11">Heb. xi. 11</reference>. It was the modest usage of that time that the women did not sit at meat with men, at least not with strangers, but confined themselves to their own apartments; therefore Sarah is here out of sight: but she must not be out of hearing. The angels enquire (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Where is Sarah thy wife?</hi> By naming her, they gave intimation enough to Abraham that, though they seemed strangers, yet they very well knew him and his family. By enquiring after her, they showed a friendly kind concern for the family and relations of one whom they found respectful to them. It is a piece of common civility, which ought to proceed from a principle of Christian love, and then it is sanctified. And, by speaking of her (she over-hearing it), they drew her to listen to what was further to be said. <hi type="italic">Where is Sarah thy wife?</hi> say the angels. "<hi type="italic">Behold in the tent,</hi>" says Abraham. "Where should she be else? There she is in her place, as she uses to be, and is now within call." Note, 1. The daughters of Sarah must learn of her to be <hi type="italic">chaste, keepers at home,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.2.5">Tit. ii. 5</reference>. There is nothing got by gadding. 2. Those are most likely to receive comfort from God and his promises that are in their place and in the way of their duty, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.8">Luke ii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen662" type="x-p"/> II. The promise is then renewed and ratified, that she should have a son (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will certainly return unto thee,</hi> and visit thee next time with the performance, as now I do with the promise." God will return to those that bid him welcome, that entertain his visits: "I will return thy kindness, <hi type="italic">Sarah thy wife shall have a son;</hi>" it is repeated again, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.14">v. 14</reference>. Thus the promises of the Messiah were often repeated in the Old Testament, for the strengthening of the faith of God's people. We are slow of heart to believe, and therefore have need of line upon line to the same purport. This is that word of promise which the apostle quotes (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.9">Rom. ix. 9</reference>), as that by the virtue of which Isaac was born. Note, 1. The same blessings which others have from common providence believers have from the promise, which makes them very sweet and very sure. 2. The spiritual seed of Abraham owe their life, and joy, and hope, and all, to the promise. They are born by the word of God, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.23">1 Pet. i. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen663" type="x-p"/> III. Sarah thinks this too good news to be true, and therefore cannot as yet find in her heart to believe it: <hi type="italic">Sarah laughed within herself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.12">v. 12</reference>. It was not a pleasing laughter of faith, like Abraham's (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.17">ch. xvii. 17</reference>), but it was a laughter of doubting and mistrust. Note, The same thing may be done from very different principles, of which God only, who knows the heart, can judge. The great objection which Sarah could not get over was her age: "<hi type="italic">I am waxed old,</hi> and past childbearing in the course of nature, especially having been hitherto barren, and (which magnifies the difficulty) <hi type="italic">my lord is old also.</hi>" Observe here, 1. Sarah calls Abraham her <hi type="italic">lord;</hi> it was the only good word in this saying, and the Holy Ghost takes notice of it to her honour, and recommends it to the imitation of all Christian wives. <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.6">1 Pet. iii. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord,</hi> in token of respect and subjection. Thus must the wife reverence her husband, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.33">Eph. v. 33</reference>. And thus must we be apt to take notice of what is spoken decently and well, to the honour of those that speak it, though it may be mixed with that which is amiss, over which we should cast a mantle of love. 2. Human improbability often sets up in contradiction to the divine promise. The objections of sense are very apt to stumble and puzzle the weak faith even of true believers. It is hard to cleave to the first Cause, when second causes frown. 3. Even where there is true faith, yet there are often sore conflicts with unbelief, Sarah could say, <hi type="italic">Lord, I believe</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.11">Heb. xi. 11</reference>), and yet must say, <hi type="italic">Lord, help my unbelief.</hi> <div eID="gen663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen664" type="x-p"/> IV. The angel reproves the indecent expressions of her distrust, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.13-Gen.18.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Observe, 1. Though Sarah was now most kindly and generously entertaining these angels, yet, when she did amiss, they reproved her for it, as Christ reproved Martha in her own house, <reference osisRef="Luke.10.40-Luke.10.41">Luke x. 40, 41</reference>. If our friends be kind to us, we must not therefore be so unkind to them as to suffer sin upon them. 2. God gave this reproof to Sarah by Abraham her husband. To him he said, <hi type="italic">Why did Sarah laugh?</hi> perhaps because he had not told her of the promise which had been given him some time before to this purport, and which, if he had communicated it to her with its ratifications, would have prevented her from being so surprised now. Or Abraham was told of it that he might tell her of it. Mutual reproof, when there is occasion for it, is one of the duties of the conjugal relation. 3. The reproof itself is plain, and backed with a good reason: <hi type="italic">Wherefore did Sarah laugh?</hi> Note, It is good to enquire into the reason of our laughter, that it may not be the laughter of the fool, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.6">Eccl. vii. 6</reference>. "Wherefore did I laugh?" Again, Our unbelief and distrust are a great offence to the God of heaven. He justly takes it ill to have the objections of sense set up in contradiction to his promise, as <reference osisRef="Luke.1.18">Luke i. 18</reference>. 4. Here is a question asked which is enough to answer all the cavils of flesh and blood: <hi type="italic">Is any thing too hard for the Lord?</hi> (Heb. <hi type="italic">too wonderful</hi>), that is, (1.) Is any thing so secret as to escape his cognizance? No, not Sarah's laughing, though it was only <hi type="italic">within herself.</hi> Or, (2.) Is any thing so difficult as to exceed his power? No, not the giving of a child to Sarah in her old age. <div eID="gen664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen665" type="x-p"/> V. Sarah foolishly endeavours to conceal her fault (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">She denied, saying, I did not laugh,</hi> thinking nobody could contradict her: she told this lie, because <hi type="italic">she was afraid;</hi> but it was in vain to attempt concealing it from an all-seeing eye; she was told, to her shame, <hi type="italic">Thou didst laugh.</hi> Now, 1. There seems to be in Sarah a retraction of her distrust. Now she perceived, by laying circumstances together, that it was a divine promise which had been made concerning her, she renounced all doubting distrustful thoughts about it. But, 2. There was withal a sinful attempt to cover a sin with a lie. It is a shame to do amiss, but a greater shame to deny it; for thereby we add iniquity to our iniquity. Fear of a rebuke often betrays us into this snare. See <reference osisRef="Isa.57.11">Isa. lvii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whom hast thou feared, that thou hast lied?</hi> But we deceive ourselves if we think to impose upon God; he can and will bring truth to light, to our shame. <hi type="italic">He that covers his sin cannot prosper,</hi> for the day is coming which will discover it.
entries.a675920fa666cdefbac90b55cf57b02b5c4c88a5: <div eID="gen665" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Abraham's Interview with God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1898.)</title> <div sID="gen666" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And the men rose up from thence, and looked toward Sodom: and Abraham went with them to bring them on the way. 17 And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, Shall I hide from Abraham that thing which I do; <hi type="super">18</hi> Seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him? <hi type="super">19</hi> For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to do justice and judgment; that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> may bring upon Abraham that which he hath spoken of him. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous; <hi type="super">21</hi> I will go down now, and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry of it, which is come unto me; and if not, I will know. 22 And the men turned their faces from thence, and went toward Sodom: but Abraham stood yet before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen667" type="x-p"/> The messengers from heaven had now despatched one part of their business, which was an errand of grace to Abraham and Sarah, and which they delivered first; but now they have before them work of another nature. Sodom is to be destroyed, and they must do it, <reference osisRef="Gen.19.13">ch. xix. 13</reference>. Note, As with the Lord there is mercy, so he is the God to whom vengeance belongs. Pursuant to their commission, we here find, 1. That <hi type="italic">they looked towards Sodom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.16">v. 16</reference>); they set their faces against it in wrath, as God is said to look unto the host of the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.24">Exod. xiv. 24</reference>. Note, Though God has long seemed to connive at sinners, from which they have inferred that the Lord does not see, does not regard, yet, when the day of his wrath comes, he will look towards them. 2. That they <hi type="italic">went towards Sodom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.22">v. 22</reference>), and accordingly we find two of them at Sodom, <reference osisRef="Gen.19.1">ch. xix. 1</reference>. Whether the third was the Lord, before whom Abraham yet stood, and to whom he drew near (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.23">v. 23</reference>), as most think, or whether the third left them before they came to Sodom, and the Lord before whom Abraham stood was the <hi type="italic">shechinah,</hi> or that appearance of the divine glory which Abraham had formerly seen and conversed with, is uncertain. However, we have here, <div eID="gen667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen668" type="x-p"/> I. The honour Abraham did to his guests: <hi type="italic">He went with them to bring them on the way,</hi> as one that was loth to part with such good company, and was desirous to pay his utmost respects to them. This is a piece of civility proper to be shown to our friends; but it must be done as the apostle directs (<reference osisRef="3John.1.6">3 John 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">after a godly sort.</hi> <div eID="gen668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen669" type="x-p"/> II. The honour they did to him; for those that honour God he will honour. God communicated to Abraham his purpose to destroy Sodom, and not only so, but entered into a free conference with him about it. Having taken him, more closely than before, into covenant with himself (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.1-Gen.17.23">ch. xvii.</reference>), he here admits him into more intimate communion with himself than ever, as the man of his counsel. Observe here, <div eID="gen669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen670" type="x-p"/> 1. God's friendly thoughts concerning Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.17-Gen.18.19">v. 17-19</reference>, where we have his resolution to make known to Abraham his purpose concerning Sodom, with the reasons of it. If Abraham had not brought them on their way, perhaps he would not have been thus favoured; but he that loves to walk with wise men shall be wise, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.20">Prov. xiii. 20</reference>. See how God is pleased to argue with himself: <hi type="italic">Shall I hide from Abraham</hi> (or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">Am I concealing from Abraham</hi>) <hi type="italic">that thing which I do?</hi> "Can I go about such a thing, and not tell Abraham?" Thus does God, in his counsels, express himself, after the manner of men, with deliberation. But why must Abraham be of the cabinet-council? The Jews suggest that because God had granted the land of Canaan to Abraham and his seed therefore he would not destroy those cities which were a part of that land, without his knowledge and consent. But God here gives two other reasons:— <div eID="gen670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen671" type="x-p"/> (1.) Abraham must know, for he is a friend and a favourite, and one that God has a particular kindness for and great things in store for. He is to become a great nation; and not only so, but in the Messiah, who is to come from his loins, <hi type="italic">All nations of the earth shall be blessed.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">The secret of the Lord is with those that fear him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Ps. xxv. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.32">Prov. iii. 32</reference>. Those who by faith live a life of communion with God cannot but know more of his mind than other people, though not with a prophetical, yet with a prudential practical knowledge. They have a better insight than others into what is present (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.9">Hos. xiv. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.43">Ps. cvii. 43</reference>), and a better foresight of what is to come, at least so much as suffices for their guidance and for their comfort. <div eID="gen671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen672" type="x-p"/> (2.) Abraham must know, for he will teach his household: <hi type="italic">I know Abraham</hi> very well, that <hi type="italic">he will command his children and his household after him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">v. 19</reference>. Consider this, [1.] As a very bright part of Abraham's character and example. He not only prayed with his family, but he taught them as a man of knowledge, nay, he commanded them as a man in authority, and was prophet and king, as well as priest, in his own house. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> God having made the covenant with him and his seed, and his household being circumcised pursuant to that, he was very careful to teach and rule them well. Those that expect family blessings must make conscience of family duty. If our children be the Lord's, they must be nursed for him; if they wear his livery, they must be trained up in his work. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Abraham took care not only of his children, but of his household; his servants were catechized servants. Masters of families should instruct and inspect the manners of all under their roof. The poorest servants have precious souls that must be looked after. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Abraham made it his care and business to promote practical religion in his family. He did not fill their heads with matters of nice speculation, or doubtful disputation; but he taught them to keep <hi type="italic">the way of the Lord, and to do judgment and justice,</hi> that is, to be serious and devout in the worship of God and to be honest in their dealings with all men. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> Abraham, herein, had an eye to posterity, and was in care not only that his household with him, but that his household after him, should keep the way of the Lord, that religion might flourish in his family when he was in his grave. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> His doing this was the fulfilling of the conditions of the promises which God had made him. Those only can expect the benefit of the promises that make conscience of their duty. [2.] As the reason why God would make known to him his purpose concerning Sodom, because he was communicative of his knowledge, and improved it for the benefit of those that were under his charge. Note, To him that hath shall be given, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.12">Matt. xiii. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.29">xxv. 29</reference>. Those that make a good use of their knowledge shall know more. <div eID="gen672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen673" type="x-p"/> 2. God's friendly talk with Abraham, in which he makes known to him purpose concerning Sodom, and allows him a liberty of application to him about the matter. (1.) He tells him of the evidence there was against Sodom: <hi type="italic">The cry of Sodom is great,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.20">v. 20</reference>. Note, Some sins, and the sins of some sinners, cry aloud to heaven for vengeance. The iniquity of Sodom was crying iniquity, that is, it was so very provoking that it even urged God to punish. (2.) The enquiry he would make upon this evidence: <hi type="italic">I will go down now and see,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.21">v. 21</reference>. Not as if there were any thing concerning which God is in doubt, or in the dark; but he is pleased thus to express himself after the manner of men, [1.] To show the incontestable equity of all his judicial proceedings. Men are apt to suggest that his way is not equal; but let them know that his judgments are the result of an eternal counsel, and are never rash or sudden resolves. He never punishes upon report, or common fame, or the information of others, but upon his own certain and infallible knowledge. [2.] To give example to magistrates, and those in authority, with the utmost care and diligence to enquire into the merits of a cause, before they give judgment upon it. [3.] Perhaps the decree is here spoken of as not yet peremptory, that room and encouragement might be given to Abraham to make intercession for them. Thus God looked if there were any to intercede, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.16">Isa. lix. 16</reference>.
entries.1fafa48adf450833a70fc0275a9e977bfa0a5c45: <div eID="gen673" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Abraham's Intercession for Sodom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1898.)</title> <div sID="gen674" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> And Abraham drew near, and said, Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked? <hi type="super">24</hi> Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city: wilt thou also destroy and not spare the place for the fifty righteous that <hi type="italic">are</hi> therein? <hi type="super">25</hi> That be far from thee to do after this manner, to slay the righteous with the wicked: and that the righteous should be as the wicked, that be far from thee: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? <hi type="super">26</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare all the place for their sakes. 27 And Abraham answered and said, Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which <hi type="italic">am but</hi> dust and ashes: 28 Peradventure there shall lack five of the fifty righteous: wilt thou destroy all the city for <hi type="italic">lack of</hi> five? And he said, If I find there forty and five, I will not destroy <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">29</hi> And he spake unto him yet again, and said, Peradventure there shall be forty found there. And he said, I will not do <hi type="italic">it</hi> for forty's sake. <hi type="super">30</hi> And he said <hi type="italic">unto him,</hi> Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak: Peradventure there shall thirty be found there. And he said, I will not do <hi type="italic">it,</hi> if I find thirty there. <hi type="super">31</hi> And he said, Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord: Peradventure there shall be twenty found there. And he said, I will not destroy <hi type="italic">it</hi> for twenty's sake. <hi type="super">32</hi> And he said, Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak yet but this once: Peradventure ten shall be found there. And he said, I will not destroy <hi type="italic">it</hi> for ten's sake. <hi type="super">33</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> went his way, as soon as he had left communing with Abraham: and Abraham returned unto his place. <div eID="gen674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen675" type="x-p"/> Communion with God is kept up by the word and by prayer. In the word God speaks to us; in prayer we speak to him. God had revealed to Abraham his purposes concerning Sodom; now from this Abraham takes occasion to speak to God on Sodom's behalf. Note, God's word then does us good when it furnishes us with matter for prayer and excites us to it. When God has spoken to us, we must consider what we have to say to him upon it. Observe, <div eID="gen675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen676" type="x-p"/> I. The solemnity of Abraham's address to God on this occasion: <hi type="italic">Abraham drew near,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.23">v. 23</reference>. The expression intimates, 1. A holy concern: <hi type="italic">He engaged his heart</hi> to approach to God, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer. xxx. 21</reference>. "Shall Sodom be destroyed, and I not speak one good word for it?" 2. A holy confidence: He drew near <hi type="italic">with an assurance of faith,</hi> drew near <hi type="italic">as a prince,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.37">Job xxxi. 37</reference>. Note, When we address ourselves to the duty of prayer, we ought to remember that we are drawing near to God, that we may be filled with a reverence of him, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.3">Lev. x. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen677" type="x-p"/> II. The general scope of this prayer. It is the first solemn prayer we have upon record in the Bible; and it is a prayer for the sparing of Sodom. Abraham, no doubt, greatly abhorred the wickedness of the Sodomites; he would not have lived among them, as Lot did, if they would have given him the best estate in their country; and yet he prayed earnestly for them. Note, Though sin is to be hated, sinners are to be pitied and prayed for. God delights not in their death, nor should we desire, but deprecate, the woeful day. 1. He begins with a prayer that the righteous among them might be spared, and not involved in the common calamity, having an eye particularly to just Lot, whose disingenuous carriage towards him he had long since forgiven and forgotten, witness his friendly zeal to rescue him before by his sword and now by his prayers. 2. He improves this into a petition that all might be spared for the sake of the righteous that were among them, God himself countenancing this request, and in effect putting him upon it by his answer to his first address, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.26">v. 26</reference>. Note, We must pray, not only for ourselves, but for others also; for we are members of the same body, at least of the same body of mankind. <hi type="italic">All we are brethren.</hi> <div eID="gen677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen678" type="x-p"/> III. The particular graces eminent in this prayer. <div eID="gen678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen679" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is great faith; and it is the prayer of faith that is the prevailing prayer. His faith pleads with God, orders the cause, and fills his mouth with arguments. He acts faith especially upon the righteousness of God, and is very confident. <div eID="gen679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen680" type="x-p"/> (1.) That God will not <hi type="italic">destroy the righteous with the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.23">v. 23</reference>. No, <hi type="italic">that be far from thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.25">v. 25</reference>. We must never entertain any thought that derogates from the honour of God's righteousness. See <reference osisRef="Rom.3.5-Rom.3.6">Rom. iii. 5, 6</reference>. Note, [1.] The righteous are mingled with the wicked in this world. Among the best there are, commonly, some bad, and among the worst some good: even in Sodom, one Lot. [2.] Though the righteous be among the wicked, yet the righteous God will not, certainly he will not, destroy the righteous with the wicked. Though in this world they may be involved in the same common calamities, yet in the great day a distinction with be made. <div eID="gen680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen681" type="x-p"/> (2.) That the righteous shall not <hi type="italic">be as the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.25">v. 25</reference>. Though they may suffer with them, yet they do not suffer like them. Common calamities are quite another thing to the righteous than what they are to the wicked, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.7">Isa. xxvii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen682" type="x-p"/> (3.) That <hi type="italic">the Judge of all the earth will do right;</hi> undoubtedly he will, because he is the Judge of all the earth; it is the apostle's argument, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.5-Rom.3.6">Rom. iii. 5, 6</reference>. Note, [1.] God is the Judge of all the earth; he gives charge to all, takes cognizance of all, and will pass sentence upon all. [2.] That God Almighty never did nor ever will do any wrong to any of the creatures, either by withholding that which is right or by exacting more than is right, <reference osisRef="Job.34.10-Job.34.11">Job xxxiv. 10, 11</reference>. <div eID="gen682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen683" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is great humility. <div eID="gen683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen684" type="x-p"/> (1.) A deep sense of his own unworthiness (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, who am but dust and ashes;</hi> and again, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.31">v. 31</reference>. He speaks as one amazed at his own boldness, and the liberty God graciously allowed him, considering God's greatness—he is <hi type="italic">the Lord;</hi> and his own meanness—<hi type="italic">but dust and ashes.</hi> Note, [1.] The greatest of men, the most considerable and deserving, are but dust and ashes, mean and vile before God, despicable, frail, and dying. [2.] Whenever we draw near to God, it becomes us reverently to acknowledge the vast distance that there is between us and God. He is the Lord of glory, we are worms of the earth. [3.] The access we have to the throne of grace, and the freedom of speech allowed us, are just matter of humble wonder, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18">2 Sam. vii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen685" type="x-p"/> (2.) An awful dread of God's displeasure: <hi type="italic">O let not the Lord be angry</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.30">v. 30</reference>), and again, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.32">v. 32</reference>. Note, [1.] The importunity which believers use in their addresses to God is such that, if they were dealing with a man like themselves, they could not but fear that he would be angry with them. But he with whom we have to do is <hi type="italic">God and not man;</hi> and, whoever he may seem, is not really <hi type="italic">angry with the prayers of the upright</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.4">Ps. lxxx. 4</reference>), for they are <hi type="italic">his delight</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.15.8">Prov. xv. 8</reference>), and he is pleased when he is wrestled with. [2.] That even when we receive special tokens of the divine favour we ought to be jealous over ourselves, lest we make ourselves obnoxious to the divine displeasure; and therefore we must bring the Mediator with us in the arms of our faith, to atone for <hi type="italic">the iniquity of our holy things.</hi> <div eID="gen685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen686" type="x-p"/> 3. Here is great charity. (1.) A charitable opinion of Sodom's character: as bad as it was, he thought there were several good people in it. It becomes us to hope the best of the worst places. Of the two it is better to err in that extreme. (2.) A charitable desire of Sodom's welfare: he used all his interest at the throne of grace for mercy for them. We never find him thus earnest in pleading with God for himself and his family, as here for Sodom. <div eID="gen686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen687" type="x-p"/> 4. Here are great boldness and believing confidence. (1.) He took the liberty to pitch upon a certain number of righteous ones which he supposed might be in Sodom. Suppose there be fifty, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.24">v. 24</reference>. (2.) He advanced upon God's concessions, again and again. As God granted much, he still begged more, with the hope of gaining his point. (3.) He brought the terms as low as he could for shame (having prevailed for mercy if there were but ten righteous ones in five cities), and perhaps so low that he concluded they would have been spared. <div eID="gen687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen688" type="x-p"/> IV. The success of the prayer. He that thus wrestled prevailed wonderfully; as a prince he had power with God: it was but ask and have. 1. God's general good-will appears in this, that he consented to spare the wicked for the sake of the righteous. See how swift God is to show mercy; he even seeks a reason for it. See what great blessings good people are to any place, and how little those befriend themselves that hate and persecute them. 2. His particular favour to Abraham appeared in this, that he did not leave off granting till Abraham left off asking. Such is the power of prayer. Why then did Abraham leave off asking, when he had prevailed so far as to get the place spared it there were but ten righteous in it? Either, (1.) Because he owned that it deserved to be destroyed if there were not so many; <hi type="italic">as the dresser of the vineyard,</hi> who consented that the barren tree should be cut down if one year's trial more did not make it fruitful, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.9">Luke xiii. 9</reference>. Or, (2.) Because God restrained his spirit from asking any further. When God has determined the ruin of a place, he forbids it to be prayed for, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">Jer. vii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">xi. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.11">xiv. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen689" type="x-p"/> V. Here is the breaking up of the conference, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.33">v. 33</reference>. 1. <hi type="italic">The Lord went his way.</hi> The visions of God must not be constant in this world, where it is by faith only that we are to set God before us. God did not go away till Abraham had said all he had to say; for he is never weary of hearing prayer, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.1-Isa.59.2">Isa. lix. 1. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Abraham returned unto his place,</hi> not puffed up with the honour done him, nor by these extraordinary interviews taken off from the ordinary course of duty. He returned to his place to observe what that event would be; and it proved that his prayer was heard, and yet Sodom was not spared, because there were not ten righteous in it. We cannot expect too little from man nor too much from God.  <chapter eID="Gen.18"/> <div eID="gen689" type="x-p"/>

entries.5c8b43fdcee616bad908255b30d003587532c115: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv190"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.18.1-Gen.18.8">Ge 18:1-8</reference>. Entertainment of Angels.</title> <div sID="gen354" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv190"/><hi type="bold">1. the Lord appeared--</hi>another manifestation of the divine presence, more familiar than any yet narrated; and more like that in the fulness of time, when the Word was made flesh.<div eID="gen354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen355" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plains of Mamre--</hi>rather, terebinth or oak of Mamre; a tall-spreading tree or grove of trees.<div eID="gen355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sat in the tent door--</hi>The tent itself being too close and sultry at noon, the shaded open front is usually resorted to for the air that may be stirring. <div eID="gen356" type="x-p"/>
entries.3aaa59efdb8149cc32158a2649c5bd5754a5e208: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv191"/><div sID="gen357" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv191"/><hi type="bold">2. lift up his eyes ... and, lo, three men--</hi>Travellers in that quarter start at sunrise and continue till midday when they look out for some resting-place.<div eID="gen357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he ran to meet them--</hi>When the visitor is an ordinary person, the host merely rises; but if of superior rank, the custom is to advance a little towards the stranger, and after a very low bow, turn and lead him to the tent, putting an arm round his waist, or tapping him on the shoulder as they go, to assure him of welcome. <div eID="gen358" type="x-p"/>
entries.854ba91e8d4f931e5f3d420b4d479305ca5b1011: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv192"/><div sID="gen359" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv192"/><hi type="bold">3. My Lord, if now I have found favor--</hi>The hospitalities offered are just of the kind that are necessary and most grateful, the refreshment of water, for feet exposed to dust and heat by the sandals, being still the first observed among the pastoral people of Hebron. <div eID="gen359" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c72d1958bfc36b72d42a866db8395ce5ebc11a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv193"/><div sID="gen360" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv193"/><hi type="bold">5. for therefore are ye come--</hi>No questions were asked. But Abraham knew their object by the course they took--approaching directly in front of the chief sheik's tent, which is always distinguishable from the rest and thus showing their wish to be his guests. <div eID="gen360" type="x-p"/>
entries.b207dca0aab3b5d11722d94392aa129784fd35ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv194"/><div sID="gen361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv194"/><hi type="bold">6. Abraham hastened ... unto Sarah ... make cakes upon the hearth--</hi>Bread is baked daily, no more than is required for family use, and always by the women, commonly the wife. It is a short process. Flour mixed with water is made into dough, and being rolled out into cakes, it is placed on the earthen floor, previously heated by a fire. The fire being removed, the cakes are laid on the ground, and being covered over with hot embers, are soon baked, and eaten the moment they are taken off. <div eID="gen361" type="x-p"/>
entries.b374b5f7cac9c7183fe363968a21fd174b83f378: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv195"/><div sID="gen362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv195"/><hi type="bold">7. Abraham ran unto the herd, and fetched a calf--</hi>Animal food is never provided, except for visitors of a superior rank when a kid or lamb is killed. A calf is still a higher stretch of hospitality, and it would probably be cooked as is usually done when haste is required--either by roasting it whole or by cutting it up into small pieces and broiling them on skewers over the fire. It is always eaten along with boiled corn swimming in butter or melted fat, into which every morsel of meat, laid upon a piece of bread, is dipped, before being conveyed by the fingers to the mouth. <div eID="gen362" type="x-p"/>
entries.74f589a54c6b1e9f8c72ed9d3c3619d9c94f3279: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv196"/><div sID="gen363" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv196"/><hi type="bold">8. milk--</hi>A bowl of camel's milk ends the repast.<div eID="gen363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he stood by them under the tree--</hi>The host himself, even though he has a number of servants, deems it a necessary act of politeness to stand while his guests are at their food, and Abraham evidently did this before he was aware of the real character of his visitors. <div eID="gen364" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ee2d07ecca3b2c693b6b776559e32a0c82a054d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv197"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.18.9-Gen.18.15">Ge 18:9-15</reference>. Reproof of Sarah. An inquiry about his wife, so surprising in strangers, the subject of conversation, and the fulfilment of the fondly cherished promise within a specified time, showed Abraham that he had been entertaining more than ordinary travellers (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.2">He 13:2</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen365" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv197"/><hi type="bold">10. Sarah heard it in the tent door, which was behind him--</hi>The women's apartment is in the back of the tent, divided by a thin partition from the men's. <div eID="gen365" type="x-p"/>
entries.3eb4557d28b94cce5392c1163d66674774b34951: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv198"/><div sID="gen366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv198"/><hi type="bold">12. Therefore Sarah laughed within herself--</hi>Long delay seems to have weakened faith. Sarah treated the announcement as incredible, and when taxed with the silent sneer, she added falsehood to distrust. It was an aggravated offense (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.4">Ac 5:4</reference>), and nothing but grace saved her (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.18">Ro 9:18</reference>). <div eID="gen366" type="x-p"/>
entries.891fd4466e429f472bbf9942dbd6881b566a0581: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv199"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.18.16-Gen.18.22">Ge 18:16-22</reference>. Disclosure of Sodom's Doom.</title> <div sID="gen367" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv199"/><hi type="bold">16. the men rose ... Abraham went with them--</hi>It is customary for a host to escort his guests a little way. <div eID="gen367" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fd748524875397212f22c979a1d823d60ff144a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv200"/><div sID="gen368" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv200"/><hi type="bold">17. the Lord said, Shall I hide--</hi>The chief stranger, no other than the Lord, disclosed to Abraham the awful doom about to be inflicted on Sodom and the cities of the plain for their enormous wickedness. <div eID="gen368" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f8c3b5651490d28ca8568bb80522503cd0b8e4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv201"/><div sID="gen369" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv201"/><hi type="bold">21. I will go down ... and see--</hi>language used after the manner of men. These cities were to be made examples to all future ages of God's severity; and therefore ample proof given that the judgment was neither rash nor excessive (<reference osisRef="Ezek.18.23">Eze 18:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.7">Jr 18:7</reference>). <div eID="gen369" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0d7a1ecfbc2a79d4a4675a28465bb7068147512: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv202"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.18.23-Gen.18.33">Ge 18:23-33</reference>. Abraham's Intercession.</title> <div sID="gen370" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv202"/><hi type="bold">23. Abraham drew near, and said, &c.--</hi>The scene described is full of interest and instruction--showing in an unmistakable manner the efficacy of prayer and intercession. (See also <reference osisRef="Prov.15.8">Pr 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.16">Jas 5:16</reference>). Abraham reasoned justly as to the rectitude of the divine procedure (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.5">Ro 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.6">6</reference>), and many guilty cities and nations have been spared on account of God's people (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.13">Mt 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.22">24:22</reference>). <div eID="gen370" type="x-p"/>
entries.32e09b56e71dde4b22fb00afc790e69e6244c9e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv203"/><div sID="gen371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv203"/><hi type="bold">33. the Lord ... left communing ... and Abraham returned unto his place--</hi>Why did Abraham cease to carry his intercessions farther? Either because he fondly thought that he was now sure of the cities being preserved (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.9">Lu 13:9</reference>), or because the Lord restrained his mind from further intercession (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">Jr 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">11:14</reference>). But there were not ten "righteous persons." There was only one, and he might without injustice have perished in the general overthrow (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.2">Ec 9:2</reference>). But a difference is sometimes made, and on this occasion the grace of God was manifested in a signal manner for the sake of Abraham. What a blessing to be connected with a saint of God! <chapter eID="Gen.18"/>

entries.0b49170eff866673599475323d12b54e3d1a8ed4: <div eID="gen827" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen828" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen829" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen829" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen828" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen830" type="x-p"/> The Lord appears unto Abraham in Mamre, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.1">Gen 18:1</reference>. Three angels, in human appearance, come towards his tent, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.2">Gen 18:2</reference>. He invites them in to wash and refresh themselves, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.3-Gen.18.5">Gen 18:3-5</reference>; prepares a calf, bread, butter, and milk, for their entertainment; and himself serves them, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.6-Gen.18.8">Gen 18:6-8</reference>. They promise that within a year Sarah shall have a son, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.9">Gen 18:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.10">Gen 18:10</reference>. Sarah, knowing herself and husband to be superannuated, smiles at the promise, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.11">Gen 18:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.12">Gen 18:12</reference>. One of the three, who is called the Lord or Jehovah, chides her, and asserts the sufficiency of the Divine power to accomplish the promise, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.13">Gen 18:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.14">Gen 18:14</reference>. Sarah, through fear, denies that she had laughed or showed signs of unbelief, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.15">Gen 18:15</reference>. Abraham accompanies these Divine persons on their way to Sodom, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.16">Gen 18:16</reference>; and that one who is called Jehovah informs him of his purpose to destroy Sodom and Gomorrah, because of their great wickedness, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.17-Gen.18.21">Gen 18:17-21</reference>. The two former proceed toward Sodom, while the latter (Jehovah) remains with Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.22">Gen 18:22</reference>. Abraham intercedes for the inhabitants of those cities, entreating the Lord to spare them provided fifty righteous persons should be found in them, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.23-Gen.18.25">Gen 18:23-25</reference>. The Lord grants this request, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.26">Gen 18:26</reference>. He pleads for the same mercy should only forty-five be found there; which is also granted, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.27">Gen 18:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.28">Gen 18:28</reference>. He pleads the same for forty, which is also granted, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.29">Gen 18:29</reference>; for thirty, with the same success, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.30">Gen 18:30</reference>; for twenty, and receives the some gracious answer, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.31">Gen 18:31</reference>; for ten, and the Lord assures him that should ten righteous persons be found there, he will not destroy the place, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.32">Gen 18:32</reference>. Jehovah then departs, and Abraham returns to his tent, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.33">Gen 18:33</reference>. <div eID="gen830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen831" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen832" type="x-p"/> And the Lord appeared - See note on <reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Gen 15:1</reference>. <div eID="gen832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen833" type="x-p"/> Sat in the tent door - For the purpose of enjoying the refreshing air in the heat of the day, when the sun had most power. A custom still frequent among the Asiatics.
entries.ea2117bcba2cb974137ba9c25899d7ff5a5ad9b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen834" type="x-p"/> Three men stood by him - נצבים עליו nitstsabim alaiv, were standing over against him; for if they had been standing by him, as our translation says, he needed not to have "run from the tent door to meet them." To Abraham these appeared at first as men; but he entertained angels unawares, see <reference osisRef="Heb.13.2">Heb 13:2</reference>.
entries.0567758bde158de329ce5d3a8eeb233616bce2e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen835" type="x-p"/> And said, My Lord, etc. - The word is אדני Adonai, not יהוה Yehovah, for as yet Abraham did not know the quality of his guests. For an explanation of this word, See note on <reference osisRef="Gen.15.8">Gen 15:8</reference>.
entries.ee3c8f79417c0a1f873ea817987e000ada9f1770: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen836" type="x-p"/> Let a little water - be fetched, and wash your feet, etc. - In these verses we find a delightful picture of primitive hospitality. In those ancient times shoes such as ours were not in use; and the foot was protected only by sandals or soles, which fastened round the foot with straps. It was therefore a great refreshment in so hot a country to get the feet washed at the end of a day's journey; and this is the first thing that Abraham proposes. <div eID="gen836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen837" type="x-p"/> Rest yourselves under the tree - We have already heard of the oak grove of Mamre, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.6">Gen 12:6</reference>, and this was the second requisite for the refreshment of a weary traveler, viz., rest in the shade.
entries.7ff9ace62dd1eb7b4c0c9e020be425895e5848be: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen838" type="x-p"/> I will fetch a morsel of bread - This was the third requisite, and is introduced in its proper order; as eating immediately after exertion or fatigue is very unwholesome. The strong action of the lungs and heart should have time to diminish before any food is received into the stomach, as otherwise concoction is prevented, and fever in a less or greater degree produced. <div eID="gen838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen839" type="x-p"/> For therefore are ye come - In those ancient days every traveler conceived he had a right to refreshment, when he needed it, at the first tent he met with on his journey. <div eID="gen839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen840" type="x-p"/> So do as thou hast said - How exceedingly simple was all this! On neither side is there any compliment but such as a generous heart and sound sense dictate.
entries.9b2897e99fe478609e64da7bdd44af2143f3cd63: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen841" type="x-p"/> Three measures of fine meal - The סאה seah, which is here translated measure, contained, according to Bishop Cumberland, about two gallons and a half; and Mr. Ainsworth translates the word peck. On this circumstance the following observations of the judicious and pious Abbe Fleury cannot fail to be acceptable to the reader. Speaking of the frugality of the patriarchs he says: "We have an instance of a splendid entertainment in that which Abraham made for the three angels. He set a whole calf before them, new bread, but baked on the hearth, together with butter and milk. Three measures of meal were baked into bread on this occasion, which come to more than two of our bushels, and nearly to fifty-six pounds of our weight; hence we may conclude that men were great eaters in those days, used much exercise, were probably of a much larger stature as well as longer lives than we. Homer (Odyss. lib. xiv., ver. 74, etc). makes his heroes great eaters. When Eumaeus entertained Ulysses, he dressed two pigs for himself and his guest. 'So saying, he girded quick his tunic close, <div eID="gen841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen842" type="x-p"/> And issuing sought the styes; thence bringing two, <div eID="gen842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen843" type="x-p"/> Of the imprisoned herd, he slaughtered both, <div eID="gen843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen844" type="x-p"/> Singed them and slash'd and spitted them, and placed <div eID="gen844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen845" type="x-p"/> The whole well roasted, banquets spits, and all, <div eID="gen845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen846" type="x-p"/> Reeking before Ulysses.' <div eID="gen846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen847" type="x-p"/> Cowper. <div eID="gen847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen848" type="x-p"/> On another occasion a hog of five years old was slaughtered and served up for five persons: - ' - His wood for fuel he prepared, <div eID="gen848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen849" type="x-p"/> And dragging thither a well-fatted brawn <div eID="gen849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen850" type="x-p"/> Of the fifth year: <div eID="gen850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen851" type="x-p"/> Next piercing him, and scorching close his hair, <div eID="gen851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen852" type="x-p"/> The joints they parted,' etc. <div eID="gen852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen853" type="x-p"/> Cowper. Ibid. ver. 419. <div eID="gen853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen854" type="x-p"/> Homer's heroes wait upon themselves and guests in the common occasions of life; the patriarchs do the same. Abraham, who had so many servants, and was nearly a hundred years old, brought the water himself to wash the feet of his guests, ordered his wife to make the bread quickly, went himself to choose the calf from the herd, and came again to serve them standing. I will allow that he was animated on this occasion with a desire of showing hospitality, but the lives of all the rest of the patriarchs were similar to this." <div eID="gen854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen855" type="x-p"/> Make cakes upon the hearth - Or under the ashes. This mode is used in the east to the present day. When the hearth is strongly heated with the fire that has been kindled on it, they remove the coals, sweep off the ashes, lay on the bread, and then cover it with the hot cinders.
entries.05349e83020b1e9ebafdcfc793dfcee47fc0f0c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen856" type="x-p"/> And he stood by them under the tree, and they did eat - Nothing is more common in Hindostan than to see travelers and guests eating under the shade of trees. Feasts are scarcely ever held in houses. The house of a Hindoo serves for sleeping and cooking, and for shutting up the women; but is never considered as a sitting or dining room - Ward.
entries.7d55ab6608c9ce852d6df5722bd4b1cad129deb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen857" type="x-p"/> I will certainly return - Abraham was now ninety-nine years of age, and this promise was fulfilled when he was a hundred; so that the phrase according to the time of life must mean either a complete year, or nine months from the present time, the ordinary time of pregnancy. Taken in this latter sense, Abraham was now in the ninety-ninth year of his age, and Isaac was born when he was in his hundredth year.
entries.d76aaf961c77eed09b35aaa8cbd97b1681eb814d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen858" type="x-p"/> It ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women - And consequently, naturally speaking, conception could not take place; therefore if she have a son it must be in a supernatural or miraculous way.
entries.46b97d997d32b9981a14de5e5310bf722496afb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen859" type="x-p"/> Sarah laughed - Partly through pleasure at the bare idea of the possibility of the thing, and partly from a conviction that it was extremely improbable. She appears to have been in the same spirit, and to have had the same feelings of those who, unexpectedly hearing of something of great consequence to themselves, smile and say, "The news is too good to be true;", see <reference osisRef="Gen.21.6">Gen 21:6</reference>. There is a case very similar to this mentioned <reference osisRef="Psa.126.1">Psa 126:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.126.2">Psa 126:2</reference>. On Abraham's laughing, See note on <reference osisRef="Gen.17.17">Gen 17:17</reference>.
entries.9c186e56a5557075458066aa27f97b3dc63389ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen860" type="x-p"/> And the Lord (Jehovah) said, etc. - So it appears that one of those three persons was Jehovah, and as this name is never given to any created being, consequently the ever-blessed God is intended; and as he was never seen in any bodily shape, consequently the great Angel of the covenant, Jesus Christ, must be meant. See note on <reference osisRef="Gen.16.7">Gen 16:7</reference>.
entries.b7ac32cda72556e92193bc0831c1bc25663f55ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen861" type="x-p"/> Is any thing too hard for the Lord? - היפלא מיהוה דבר hayippale meihovah dabar, shall a word (or thing) be wonderful from the Lord? i.e., Can any thing be too great a miracle for him to effect? The Septuagint translate the passage, Μη αδυνατησει παρα τῳ Θεῳ ῥημα; which St. Luke adopts almost literatim, only making it an affirmative position instead of a question: Ουκ αδυνατησει παρα τῳ Θεῳ παν ῥημα, which we translate, "With God nothing shall be impossible," <reference osisRef="Luk.1.37">Luk 1:37</reference>. Many copies of the Septuagint insert the word παν before ῥημα, as in St. Luke; but it makes little difference in the sense. It was to correct Sarah's unbelief, and to strengthen her faith, that God spoke these most important words; words which state that where human wisdom, prudence, and energy fall, and where nature herself ceases to be an agent, through lack of energy to act, or laws to direct and regulate energy, there also God has full sway, and by his own omnific power works all things after the counsel of his own will. Is there an effect to be produced? God can produce it as well without as with means. He produced nature, the whole system of causes and effects, when in the whole compass of his own eternity there was neither means nor being. He spake, and it was done; He commanded, and it stood fast. How great and wonderful is God!
entries.26f072aaffd200e20c9234a59edefba0524d7120: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen862" type="x-p"/> Abraham went with them to bring them on the way - This was another piece of primitive hospitality - to direct strangers in the way. Public roads did not then exist and guides were essentially necessary in countries where villages were seldom to be met with, and where solitary dwellings did not exist.
entries.0862c222b2bbb8bd180b55b7cceedb92cb148b20: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen863" type="x-p"/> Shall I hide from Abraham - That is, I will not hide. A common mode of speech in Scripture - a question asked when an affirmative is designed. Do men gather grapes of thorns? Men do not gather grapes of thorns, etc.
entries.ffff13ee6d6afbbe3c0c27e18c59882e8fc5458d: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen864" type="x-p"/> Shall surely become a great and mighty nation - The revelation that I make to him shall be preserved among his posterity; and the exact fulfillment of my promises, made so long before, shall lead them to believe in my name and trust in my goodness.
entries.bfe677dda8ca033919d2508ebe8613c9fab129b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen865" type="x-p"/> And they shall keep the way of the Lord - The true religion; God's way; that in which God walks himself, and in which, of course, his followers walk also; to do justice and judgment; not only to preserve the truth in their creed, but maintain it in their practice.
entries.0d9bf1e62fd4124ea11cb3d822f2f8fc34a2435a: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen866" type="x-p"/> Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah - See note on <reference osisRef="Gen.13.13">Gen 13:13</reference>.
entries.ae3797275768a2936de2cc2956ee2ae99e158bbd: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen867" type="x-p"/> I will go down now, etc. - A lesson to magistrates, teaching them not to judge according to report, but accurately to inquire into the facts themselves - Jarchi.
entries.ca528f2fef8a6d830a821b7380e78c17347493da: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen868" type="x-p"/> And the men turned their faces - That is, the two angels who accompanied Jehovah were now sent towards Sodom; while the third, who is called the Lord or Jehovah, remained with Abraham for the purpose of teaching him the great usefulness and importance of faith and prayer.
entries.209bc804e673787cbec38cf905fe8274c76c9a68: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen869" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked? - A form of speech similar to that in <reference osisRef="Gen.18.17">Gen 18:17</reference>, an invariable principle of justice, that the righteous shall not be punished for the crimes of the impious. And this Abraham lays down as the foundation of his supplications. Who can pray with any hope of success who cannot assign a reason to God and his conscience for the petitions he offers? The great sacrifice offered by Christ is an infinite reason why a penitent sinner should expect to find the mercy for which he pleads.
entries.f6a46d20512fb29d61b156fd406476b0784fb4cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen870" type="x-p"/> Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? - God alone is the Judge of all men. Abraham, in thus addressing himself to the person in the text, considers him either as the Supreme Being or his representative.
entries.bc4d15086139159d880dfdddd5d3452b6be5979d: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen871" type="x-p"/> Which am but dust and ashes - עפר ואפר aphar vaepher, words very similar in sound, as they refer to matters which so much resemble each other. Dust - the lightest particles of earth. Ashes - the residuum of consumed substances. By these expressions he shows how deeply his soul was humbled in the presence of God. He who has high thoughts of himself must have low thoughts of the dignity of the Divine nature, of the majesty of God, and the sinfulness of sin.
entries.d9cfc273c8f37585be62c708d6503ec13d157881: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen872" type="x-p"/> Peradventure ten shall be found there - Knowing that in the family of his nephew the true religion was professed and practiced, he could not suppose there could be less than ten righteous persons in the city, he did not think it necessary to urge his supplication farther; he therefore left off his entreaties, and the Lord departed from him. It is highly worthy of observation, that while he continued to pray the presence of God was continued; and when Abraham ended, "the glory of the Lord was lifted up," as the Targum expresses it. <div eID="gen872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen873" type="x-p"/> This chapter, though containing only the preliminaries to the awful catastrophe detailed in the next, affords us several lessons of useful and important information. <div eID="gen873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen874" type="x-p"/> 1. The hospitality and humanity of Abraham are worthy, not only of our most serious regard, but also of our imitation. He sat in the door of his tent in the heat of the day, not only to enjoy the current of refreshing air, but that if he saw any weary and exhausted travelers he might invite them to rest and refresh themselves. Hospitality is ever becoming in one human being towards another; for every destitute man is a brother in distress, and demands our most prompt and affectionate assistance, according to that heavenly precept, "What ye would that men should do unto you, do even so unto them." From this conduct of Abraham a Divine precept is formed: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares. <reference osisRef="Heb.13.2">Heb 13:2</reference>. <div eID="gen874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen875" type="x-p"/> 2. Whatever is given on the ground of humanity and mercy is given unto God, and is sure to meet with his approbation and a suitable reward. While Abraham entertained his guests God discovers himself, and reveals to him the counsels of his will, and renews the promise of a numerous posterity. Sarah, though naturally speaking past child-bearing, shall have a son: natural obstacles cannot hinder the purpose of God; nature is his instrument; and as it works not only by general laws, but also by any particular will of God, so it may accomplish that will in any way he may choose to direct. It is always difficult to credit God's promises when they relate to supernatural things, and still more so when they have for their object events that are contrary to the course of nature; but as nothing is too hard for God, so "all things are possible to him that believeth." It is that faith alone which is of the operation of God's Spirit, that is capable of crediting supernatural things; he who does not pray to be enabled to believe, or, if he do, uses not the power when received, can never believe to the saving of the soul. <div eID="gen875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen876" type="x-p"/> 3. Abraham trusts much in God, and God reposes much confidence in Abraham. He knows that God is faithful, and will fulfill his promises; and God knows that Abraham is faithful, and will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the Lord to do justice and judgment; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Gen 18:19</reference>. No man lives unto himself; and God gives us neither spiritual nor temporal blessings for ourselves alone; our bread we are to divide with the hungry, and to help the stranger in distress. He who understands the way of God should carefully instruct his household in that way; and he who is the father of a family should pray to God to teach him, that he may teach his household. His ignorance of God and salvation can be no excuse for his neglecting his family: it is his indispensable duty to teach them; and God will teach him, if he earnestly seek it, that he may be able to discharge this duty to his family. Reader, if thy children or servants perish through thy neglect, God will judge thee for it in the great day. <div eID="gen876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen877" type="x-p"/> 4. The sin of Sodom and the cities of the plain was great and grievous; the measure of their iniquity was full, and God determined to destroy them. Judgment is God's strange work, but though rarely done it must be done sometimes, lest men should suppose that right and wrong, vice and virtue, are alike in the eye of God. And these judgments must be dispensed in such a way as to show they are not the results of natural causes, but come immediately from the incensed justice of the Most High. <div eID="gen877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen878" type="x-p"/> 5. Every man who loves God loves his neighbor also; and he who loves his neighbor will do all in his power to promote the well-being both of his soul and his body. Abraham cannot prevent the men of Sodom from sinning against God; but he can make prayer and intercession for their souls, and plead, if not in arrest, yet in mitigation, of judgment. He therefore intercedes for the transgressors, and God is well pleased with his intercessions. These are the offspring of God's own love in the heart of his servant. <div eID="gen878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen879" type="x-p"/> 6. How true is that word, The energetic faithful prayer of a righteous man availeth much! Abraham draws near to God by affection and faith, and in the most devout and humble manner makes prayer and supplication; and every petition is answered on the spot. Nor does God cease to promise to show mercy till Abraham ceases to intercede! What encouragement does this hold out to them that fear God, to make prayer and intercession for their sinful neighbors and ungodly relatives! Faith in the Lord Jesus endues prayer with a species of omnipotence; whatsoever a man asks of the Father in his name, he will do it. Prayer has been termed the gate of heaven, but without faith that gate cannot be opened. He who prays as he should, and believes as he ought, shall have the fullness of the blessings of the Gospel of peace.  <chapter eID="Gen.18"/> <div eID="gen879" type="x-p"/>

entries.830c539bdd6ed4d3f7899387f498fc1382ed0e3c: <div eID="gen247" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Visit of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, With Two Angels, to Abraham’s Tent - Genesis 18</title> <div sID="gen248" type="x-p"/> Having been received into the covenant with God through the rite of circumcision, Abraham was shortly afterwards honoured by being allowed to receive and entertain the Lord and two angels in his tent. This fresh manifestation of God had a double purpose, viz., to establish Sarah’s faith in the promise that she should bear a son in her old age (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.1-Gen.18.15">Gen 18:1-15</reference>), and to announce the judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah (vv. 16-33). <div eID="gen248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen249" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.1-Gen.18.5">Gen 18:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen250" type="x-p"/> When sitting, about mid-day, in the grove of Mamre, in front of his tent, Abraham looked up and unexpectedly saw three men standing at some distance from him (עליו above him, looking down upon him as he sat), viz., <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.13">Gen 18:13</reference>) and <hi type="italic">two</hi> <hi type="italic">angels</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.1">Gen 19:1</reference>); all three in human form. Perceiving at once that one of them was the Lord (אדני, i.e., God), he prostrated himself reverentially before them, and entreated them not to pass him by, but to suffer him to entertain them as his guests: “<hi type="italic">Let a little water be fetched, and wash your feet, and recline yourselves </hi>(השּׁען( sevle to recline, leaning upon the arm) <hi type="italic">under</hi> <hi type="italic">the tree</hi>.” - “<hi type="italic">Comfort your hearts:</hi>” lit., “<hi type="italic">strengthen the heart,</hi>” i.e., refresh yourselves by eating and drinking (Jdg 19:5; 1Ki 21:7). “<hi type="italic">For therefore</hi> (sc., to give me an opportunity to entertain you hospitably) <hi type="italic">have ye come over to your servant:</hi>” כּן על כּי does not stand for כּי כּן על (<hi type="italic">Ges. thes.</hi> p. 682), but means “because for this purpose” (vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §353).
entries.aab97e8ecb0307122b113b3710f1389d915c3f0e: <reference osisRef="Gen.18.6-Gen.18.8">Gen 18:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen251" type="x-p"/> When the three men had accepted the hospitable invitation, Abraham, just like a Bedouin sheikh of the present day, directed his wife to take three seahs (374 cubic inches each) of fine meal, and back cakes of it as quickly as possible (עגּות round unleavened cakes baked upon hot stones); he also had a tender calf killed, and sent for milk and butter, or curdled milk, and thus prepared a bountiful and savoury meal, of which the guests partook. The eating of material food on the part of these heavenly beings was not in appearance only, but was really eating; an act which may be attributed to the corporeality assumed, and is to be regarded as analogous to the eating on the part of the risen and glorified Christ (Luk 24:41.), although the miracle still remains physiologically incomprehensible.
entries.6e70f957fe82a016cbf1abbeb4983569d59062fc: <reference osisRef="Gen.18.9-Gen.18.15">Gen 18:9-15</reference> <div eID="gen251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen252" type="x-p"/> During the meal, at which Abraham stood, and waited upon them as the host, they asked for Sarah, for whom the visit was chiefly intended.
